title: Ullambana
hookLine: the Chinese festival of offering for ancestors, from Moggallana's mother

cards: Paper slips cover a long wall in a Chinese temple hall, row after row, each with a name brushed onto it. Some names belong to the dead: a grandfather, a mother, a baby who didn't live long.
Some belong to the living: a sick father, a child taking exams. In front of the wall, tables are heaped with fruit, rice, flowers and cloth. Monks file in and chant.
This is the Ullambana assembly, held in the seventh lunar month. You've met its Japanese cousin, Obon, with its fires and dances.
Today, stay in the Chinese hall, and ask why the wall holds the names of the living as well as the dead.

teach.b: First, the story, told a few days ago at the home altar. In the Ullambana Sutra, a Chinese Buddhist scripture, the disciple Moggallana finds his dead mother among the hungry ghosts and can't feed her himself.

The Buddha sends him to give, on the day the monks finish their summer retreat, to the whole community of monks: food, bowls, bedding, the things they need. Then what the sutra does next, which is easy to miss.
It doesn't stop with one mother. Moggallana asks whether other disciples, in times to come, could make the same offering for their own parents. The Buddha says yes, and widens it.

teach.h: FOR THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.

teach.b: The sutra says the same offering helps parents who are still alive, bringing them long life and freedom from illness, and it reaches back through the generations of ancestors too.
That's why the paper slips carry both kinds of names. Last, what the festival became.
The sutra ends with the Buddha telling disciples who care for their parents to make this offering every year, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
In China and across East Asia, families still bring names and offerings to temples in that month.
Some readers hear in it a festival about care that runs both ways in time: for the parents who are still here, and the ones who came before them.

how: In Chinese and other East Asian Buddhist communities, families bring offerings to temples in the seventh lunar month and register the names of deceased ancestors and living relatives, while monks chant the Ullambana assembly.

o: an offering for ancestors and living parents, given to monks
a night festival to scare hungry ghosts away with fire and noise
a funeral rite held only for those who died that year

p: where the Buddha says to give
the end of the summer retreat

s: in the sutra, the offering is only for Moggallana's own mother
he asks whether others can make it for their parents, and the Buddha widens it to them.
the sutra says the offering helps living parents too
it speaks of long life and freedom from illness for parents still alive.
Ullambana assemblies are only for people who died recently
names of long-gone ancestors and living relatives are both brought.

games.q: you're at an Ullambana assembly, writing names on paper slips. your father is alive and well. may his name go on the wall?
o: no: the wall is only for the dead.
yes: the sutra says the offering helps living parents too.
games.why: the sutra speaks of long life and freedom from illness for living parents, so both kinds of names go up.

practice: Let one parent or ancestor come to mind, living or gone, or, if no one in your family feels right, a teacher or someone who raised you; picture their face, or just their name.
Think of one small thing you could offer to others in their name, groceries for a food bank, a meal for a neighbor, an hour of help, and rest with them as you breathe.
If someone's absence weighs too much to hold alone, you can call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Ullambana. The festival of offering for ancestors and living parents, from the story of Moggallana's mother. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: for the ancestors. A name brushed on paper can hold a whole family. That's today, done.
